q: The transistor was invented in 1947 at:
explanation: Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley invented the transistor at Bell Labs in 1947.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The first microprocessor, Intel 4004, was introduced in:
explanation: Intel introduced the 4004, the first commercial microprocessor, in 1971.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The integrated circuit (microchip) was invented in 1958 by:
explanation: Jack Kilby built the first integrated circuit at Texas Instruments in 1958.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Robert Watson-Watt invented:
explanation: Robert Watson-Watt developed radar in the 1930s; see bank item S10.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Dynamite was invented in 1867 by:
explanation: Alfred Nobel invented dynamite in 1867; his fortune later funded the Nobel Prizes.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Benjamin Franklin invented:
explanation: Franklin invented bifocal glasses; see bank item S11.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Benjamin Franklin also invented the:
explanation: Franklin invented the lightning rod; see bank item S12.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Who discovered laughing gas (nitrous oxide)?
explanation: Joseph Priestley discovered nitrous oxide (laughing gas); see bank item S13.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Who invented the safety pin?
explanation: Walter Hunt invented the safety pin in 1849 (the bank file wrongly says 1829).

subject: Everyday Science
q: The speed of a ship is measured by an instrument called a:
explanation: A ship's speed is measured with a log; see bank item S193.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The ozone layer prevents which rays from reaching the Earth?
explanation: The ozone layer blocks harmful ultraviolet rays; see bank item S16.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Soft, combustible coal is called:
explanation: Bituminous coal is soft and combustible; see bank item S17.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in:
explanation: The first Nobel Prizes were awarded in 1901, five years after Alfred Nobel's death.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Marie Curie won Nobel Prizes in which two sciences?
explanation: Marie Curie won the Physics Prize in 1903 and the Chemistry Prize in 1911.

subject: Everyday Science
q: X-rays were discovered in 1895 by:
explanation: Wilhelm Roentgen discovered X-rays in 1895; he won the first Nobel Prize in Physics in 1901.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Gunpowder was invented in:
explanation: Gunpowder was invented in China in the 9th century.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the SI unit of momentum?
explanation: Momentum = mass x velocity, so its SI unit is kilogram metre per second (kg m/s).

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the SI unit of density?
explanation: Density = mass / volume, so its SI unit is kilogram per cubic metre (kg/m3).

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the SI unit of velocity?
explanation: Velocity = displacement / time, so its SI unit is metre per second (m/s).

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the SI unit of acceleration?
explanation: Acceleration = change in velocity / time, so its SI unit is metre per second squared (m/s2).

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following is a derived SI unit?
explanation: Newton is a derived unit (kg m/s2); metre, kilogram and second are base units.

subject: Everyday Science
q: One light year is approximately equal to:
explanation: One light year is the distance light travels in one year, about 9.46 x 10^12 km.

subject: Everyday Science
q: One parsec is approximately equal to:
explanation: One parsec equals about 3.26 light years (3.09 x 10^13 km).

subject: Everyday Science
q: One nautical mile is equal to how many kilometres?
explanation: One nautical mile equals 1.852 kilometres; it is used in sea and air navigation.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the SI unit of luminous intensity?
explanation: Luminous intensity is measured in candela (cd), one of the seven SI base units.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the SI unit of the amount of substance?
explanation: The amount of substance is measured in moles (mol), one of the seven SI base units.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the SI unit of plane angle?
explanation: Plane angle is measured in radians (rad); the steradian is for solid angle.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the SI unit of solid angle?
explanation: Solid angle is measured in steradians (sr); the radian is for plane angle.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which physical quantity has the unit kilogram metre squared per second squared (kg m2/s2)?
explanation: One joule equals one kg m2/s2, and the joule is the unit of energy (and work).

subject: Everyday Science
q: One tonne is equal to how many kilograms?
explanation: One tonne equals 1,000 kilograms.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A car travels 120 km in 2 hours. What is its average speed?
explanation: Speed = distance / time = 120 / 2 = 60 km/h.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Velocity is a ___ quantity.
explanation: Velocity has both magnitude and direction, so it is a vector quantity; speed is scalar.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Newton's first law of motion is also called the law of:
explanation: The first law states that a body stays at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a force; it is the law of inertia.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Newton's second law of motion is expressed as:
explanation: Force equals mass times acceleration (F = ma); this is Newton's second law.

subject: Everyday Science
q: 'For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction' is Newton's:
explanation: The action-reaction statement is Newton's third law of motion.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The acceleration due to gravity on the surface of the Earth is approximately:
explanation: The value of g on Earth is about 9.8 m/s2 (1.6 m/s2 is the Moon's value).

subject: Everyday Science
q: Two balls of different masses are dropped from the same height in a vacuum. Which one hits the ground first?
explanation: In a vacuum there is no air resistance, so both fall with the same acceleration g and hit together.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A 2 kg object moving at 3 m/s has a momentum of:
explanation: Momentum = mass x velocity = 2 x 3 = 6 kg m/s.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The inertia of a body depends mainly on its:
explanation: Inertia is the resistance to change in motion and it increases with mass.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Friction always acts in the direction ___ to the motion of a body.
explanation: Friction opposes relative motion, so it acts opposite to the direction of motion.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In uniform circular motion, the centripetal force is directed:
explanation: Centripetal force always points toward the centre of the circular path.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A stone tied to a string is whirled in a circle. If the string suddenly breaks, the stone flies off:
explanation: Without the centripetal pull of the string, the stone continues in a straight line tangent to the circle.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The escape velocity from the surface of the Earth is approximately:
explanation: Escape velocity from Earth is about 11.2 km/s; 7.9 km/s is the orbital velocity of a low satellite.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An astronaut in orbit feels weightless mainly because the spacecraft is in:
explanation: In orbit the astronaut and the spacecraft fall freely together, so there is no normal reaction and the astronaut feels weightless.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the SI unit of impulse?
explanation: Impulse = force x time, so its unit is the newton-second (N s), equal to kg m/s.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Work is done only when:
options: A force acts perpendicular to the displacement
A force is applied but there is no displacement
There is displacement in the direction of the force
explanation: Work = force x displacement in the direction of the force; no displacement means no work.

subject: Everyday Science
q: One joule is equal to:
explanation: Work = force x distance, so 1 joule = 1 newton x 1 metre.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The kinetic energy of a moving body is given by:
explanation: Kinetic energy = 1/2 mv2, where m is mass and v is velocity.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The potential energy of a body of mass m at height h is:
explanation: Gravitational potential energy = mgh, where g is the acceleration due to gravity.

subject: Everyday Science
q: If the velocity of a body is doubled, its kinetic energy becomes:
explanation: Kinetic energy depends on v2, so doubling v makes the energy 2^2 = 4 times.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Energy can neither be created nor destroyed; it can only be changed from one form to another. This is the:
explanation: This is the law of conservation of energy, a fundamental principle of physics.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A stretched bow (ready to shoot an arrow) mainly possesses:
explanation: A stretched bow stores elastic potential energy, which becomes kinetic energy when released.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A solar cell converts light energy directly into:
explanation: A solar cell (photovoltaic cell) converts light energy into electrical energy.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Water stored behind a dam mainly possesses:
explanation: Stored water at a height has gravitational potential energy, which is converted to kinetic and then electrical energy.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A machine does 600 joules of work in 20 seconds. Its power is:
explanation: Power = work / time = 600 / 20 = 30 watts.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A machine with 80 percent efficiency is given 100 joules of input energy. Its useful output is:
explanation: Efficiency = useful output / input, so 80 percent of 100 J = 80 J of useful output.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following is NOT a form of energy?
explanation: Friction is a force, not a form of energy; heat, light and sound are forms of energy.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Light travels fastest in:
explanation: Light travels fastest in a vacuum (about 300,000 km/s) and slows down in denser media.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The speed of light in water is approximately:
explanation: Light slows to about 225,000 km/s in water (speed in vacuum divided by the refractive index 1.33).

subject: Everyday Science
q: According to the law of reflection:
options: The angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection
The angle of reflection is always zero
Light bends away from the normal
The angle of incidence is double the angle of reflection
explanation: In reflection the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, measured from the normal.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The image formed by a plane mirror is:
options: Virtual and of the same size
explanation: A plane mirror forms a virtual, upright image of the same size, laterally inverted.

subject: Everyday Science
q: When light passes from air into glass, it bends:
explanation: Going from a rarer medium (air) to a denser one (glass), light bends toward the normal.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Total internal reflection occurs when light travels from a denser to a rarer medium at an angle:
explanation: Beyond the critical angle, light cannot leave the denser medium and is totally reflected back.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A mirage (shimmering water on a hot road) is caused by:
explanation: Hot air layers near the ground refract light until total internal reflection occurs, creating a mirage.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The splitting of white light into its constituent colours is called:
explanation: Dispersion splits white light into seven colours, as seen in a prism or a rainbow.

subject: Everyday Science
q: When white light passes through a prism, it splits into how many colours?
explanation: A prism disperses white light into seven colours: violet, indigo, blue, green, yellow, orange and red (VIBGYOR).

subject: Everyday Science
q: A rainbow is formed when sunlight passes through:
explanation: Raindrops act like tiny prisms: they refract, disperse and reflect sunlight to form a rainbow.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The sky appears blue mainly because of the ___ of sunlight by air molecules.
explanation: Air molecules scatter blue light much more than other colours (Rayleigh scattering), so the sky looks blue.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The primary colours of light are:
explanation: The primary colours of light are red, green and blue; together they make white light.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Long-sight (hypermetropia) is corrected by using a ___ lens.
explanation: Hypermetropia is corrected with a convex (converging) lens, which brings the focus forward onto the retina.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Short-sight (myopia) is corrected by using a ___ lens.
explanation: Myopia is corrected with a concave (diverging) lens, which moves the focus back onto the retina.

subject: Everyday Science
q: By the sign convention used in textbooks, the focal length of a concave mirror is:
explanation: A concave mirror converges light in front of it, so its focal length is taken as negative.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Sound waves in air are:
explanation: Sound travels in air as a longitudinal wave: particles vibrate along the direction of travel.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Sound travels fastest in:
explanation: Sound travels fastest in solids: about 5,000 m/s in steel, 1,500 m/s in water and 343 m/s in air.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The speed of sound in air at about 20 C is approximately:
explanation: Sound travels at about 343 m/s in air at 20 C; it is much faster in water and steel.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Sound cannot travel through a:
explanation: Sound needs a medium, so it cannot travel through a vacuum; this is why space is silent.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The pitch of a sound depends mainly on its:
explanation: Higher frequency means higher pitch; a shrill voice has a higher frequency than a deep voice.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The loudness of a sound depends mainly on its:
explanation: Greater amplitude means a louder sound; frequency controls pitch, not loudness.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The unit used to measure the loudness (intensity level) of sound is the:
explanation: Sound intensity level is measured in decibels (dB); frequency is measured in hertz.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An echo is produced by the ___ of sound from a distant surface.
explanation: An echo is a reflected sound that returns to the listener after striking a surface.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ultrasound has a frequency above:
explanation: Sounds above 20,000 Hz are ultrasound; humans cannot hear them, but bats and dolphins use them.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bats find their way in the dark by using:
explanation: Bats emit ultrasound and listen for the echo (echolocation) to locate objects and prey.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The same note played on a sitar and a flute sounds different because of a difference in:
explanation: Timbre (quality) depends on the overtones of the sound, so different instruments sound different at the same pitch.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Heat can be transferred from the Sun to the Earth without any medium by:
explanation: Radiation needs no medium; sunlight travels through the vacuum of space by radiation.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Heat is mainly transferred through a metal rod by:
explanation: In solids, heat travels by conduction: vibrating particles pass energy to their neighbours.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Heat is transferred through liquids and gases mainly by:
explanation: In fluids, warm parts rise and cool parts sink, carrying heat by convection.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Water has its maximum density at:
explanation: Water is densest at 4 C; below this it expands as it cools, which is why ice floats.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ice floats on water because:
options: Ice is less dense than water
Ice has more mass than water
explanation: Ice is about 9 percent less dense than water, so it floats with most of its volume submerged.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The heat required to change ice at 0 C into water at 0 C (without any temperature change) is called:
explanation: Latent heat is the heat absorbed or released during a change of state at constant temperature.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following has the highest specific heat capacity?
explanation: Water has a very high specific heat (about 4,200 J/kg K), so it heats and cools slowly.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A thermometer is used to measure:
explanation: A thermometer measures temperature; heat is energy, measured in joules.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ohm's law is expressed as:
explanation: Ohm's law states that voltage equals current times resistance (V = IR).

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the SI unit of electric potential (voltage)?
explanation: Electric potential is measured in volts (V); one volt equals one joule per coulomb.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following is the best conductor of electricity?
explanation: Copper is an excellent conductor; wood and glass are insulators and steel is a poorer conductor.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Like magnetic poles:
options: Have no effect on each other
explanation: Like poles repel and unlike poles attract, the basic rule of magnetism.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Earth's magnetic field protects life on Earth by deflecting:
explanation: The magnetosphere deflects charged particles of the solar wind away from the Earth.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An electric motor converts electrical energy into:
explanation: A motor converts electrical energy into mechanical (motion) energy; a generator does the reverse.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A generator converts mechanical energy into:
explanation: A generator converts mechanical energy (rotation) into electrical energy; a motor does the reverse.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which is the nearest galaxy to our Milky Way galaxy?
explanation: The Andromeda galaxy is the nearest large galaxy to the Milky Way, about 2.5 million light years away.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which is the brightest planet as seen from the Earth?
explanation: Venus is the brightest planet in our sky; it is called the morning star and the evening star.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A lunar eclipse occurs when:
options: The Sun comes between the Earth and the Moon
The Moon comes between the Sun and the Earth
The Earth comes between the Sun and the Moon
explanation: In a lunar eclipse the Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, so the Moon darkens.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The energy of the Sun is produced by the nuclear:
explanation: The Sun produces energy by fusing hydrogen nuclei into helium, releasing enormous energy.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which is the most abundant element in the universe?
explanation: Hydrogen makes up about 75 percent of all normal matter in the universe.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which element is most abundant in the Earth's crust?
explanation: Oxygen forms about 46.6 percent of the Earth's crust by weight.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which is the most abundant metal in the Earth's crust?
explanation: Aluminium is about 8 percent of the crust, ahead of iron.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the chemical symbol of gold?
explanation: Au comes from the Latin word aurum, meaning gold.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the chemical symbol of iron?
explanation: Fe comes from the Latin word ferrum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the chemical symbol of silver?
explanation: Ag comes from the Latin word argentum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the chemical symbol of lead?
explanation: Pb comes from the Latin word plumbum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the chemical symbol of tin?
explanation: Sn comes from the Latin word stannum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the chemical symbol of mercury?
explanation: Hg comes from hydrargyrum, meaning liquid silver.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the chemical symbol of potassium?
explanation: K comes from kalium, the Latin name of potassium.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the chemical symbol of sodium?
explanation: Na comes from natrium, the Latin name of sodium.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the atomic number of carbon?
explanation: Carbon has 6 protons, so its atomic number is 6.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the atomic number of oxygen?
explanation: Oxygen has 8 protons, so its atomic number is 8.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many elements are there in the modern periodic table?
explanation: The modern periodic table lists 118 confirmed elements.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many groups are there in the modern periodic table?
explanation: The modern periodic table has 18 groups and 7 periods.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Who arranged the elements in order of atomic number?
explanation: Moseley arranged elements by atomic number in 1913; Mendeleev used atomic weight.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Noble gases belong to which group of the periodic table?
explanation: Group 18 holds helium, neon, argon, krypton, xenon and radon.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which is the lightest element?
explanation: Hydrogen, atomic number 1, is the lightest element.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which is the lightest metal?
explanation: Lithium is the lightest metal, with density about 0.53 g/cm3.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which is the heaviest naturally occurring element?
explanation: Uranium (atomic number 92) is the heaviest element found in nature.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which metal is liquid at room temperature?
explanation: Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which non-metal is liquid at room temperature?
explanation: Bromine is the only non-metal that is liquid at room temperature.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of these metals floats on water?
explanation: Lithium, sodium and potassium are less dense than water, so they float.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which metal is the best conductor of electricity?
explanation: Silver is the best electrical conductor, followed by copper.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Diamond is an allotrope of which element?
explanation: Diamond and graphite are both allotropes of carbon.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Graphite is used in pencils because it is:
explanation: Graphite is soft and its layers slide off, leaving a dark mark.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the molecular formula of buckminsterfullerene?
explanation: Buckminsterfullerene is a cage of 60 carbon atoms, C60.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of the following are the isotopes of hydrogen?
explanation: Hydrogen has three isotopes: protium (H-1), deuterium (H-2) and tritium (H-3).

subject: Everyday Science
q: Heavy water is chemically:
explanation: Heavy water is D2O, water in which hydrogen is replaced by deuterium.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Heavy water is used in nuclear reactors as a:
explanation: Heavy water slows down neutrons, so it works as a moderator in reactors.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Hard water contains dissolved salts of:
explanation: Calcium and magnesium bicarbonates make water hard.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Temporary hardness of water can be removed by:
explanation: Boiling drives off dissolved carbon dioxide and precipitates calcium carbonate.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the pH of pure water at 25 degrees Celsius?
explanation: Pure water is neutral, with pH 7 at 25 degrees Celsius.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The pH scale ranges from:
explanation: The pH scale runs from 0 (most acidic) to 14 (most alkaline).

subject: Everyday Science
q: An acid turns blue litmus paper:
explanation: Acids turn blue litmus red; bases do the opposite.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A base turns red litmus paper:
explanation: Bases turn red litmus blue.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Vinegar contains which acid?
explanation: Vinegar is a dilute solution of acetic acid, about 5 percent.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Citrus fruits contain which acid?
explanation: Citric acid gives lemons and oranges their sour taste.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Sour milk contains which acid?
explanation: Bacteria turn milk sugar into lactic acid, souring the milk.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An ant sting contains which acid?
explanation: Ants inject formic acid, which causes the burning pain.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which acid is present in the human stomach?
explanation: Dilute hydrochloric acid in gastric juice helps digest food.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which acid is known as the 'king of chemicals'?
explanation: Sulphuric acid is called the king of chemicals because of its huge industrial use.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Aqua regia is a mixture of hydrochloric acid and nitric acid in the ratio:
explanation: Aqua regia is 3 parts HCl to 1 part HNO3 and can dissolve gold.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Aqua regia can dissolve:
explanation: Aqua regia dissolves gold and platinum, which single acids cannot.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the chemical formula of baking soda?
explanation: Baking soda is sodium bicarbonate, NaHCO3.

subject: Everyday Science
q: What is the chemical formula of washing soda?
explanation: Washing soda is hydrated sodium carbonate, Na2CO3.10H2O.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Caustic soda is:
explanation: Caustic soda is NaOH, a strong alkali used in soap making.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Quick lime is:
explanation: Quick lime is CaO, made by heating limestone.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Slaked lime is:
explanation: Adding water to quick lime gives slaked lime, Ca(OH)2.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Plaster of Paris is:
explanation: Plaster of Paris is CaSO4.1/2H2O, made by heating gypsum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Gypsum is chemically:
explanation: Gypsum is CaSO4.2H2O; heating it gives plaster of Paris.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Marble, limestone and chalk are all forms of:
explanation: Marble, limestone and chalk are all calcium carbonate.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Rust is:
explanation: Rust is hydrated ferric oxide, Fe2O3.xH2O, formed by air and moisture.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Galvanization is the coating of iron with:
explanation: A zinc coating protects iron from rusting.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Zinc protects iron from rusting because zinc is:
explanation: Zinc corrodes first, giving sacrificial protection to the iron.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Stainless steel is an alloy of iron with:
explanation: Chromium gives stainless steel its rust resistance; nickel adds strength.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Brass is an alloy of copper and:
explanation: Brass is copper plus zinc; it is used for utensils and fittings.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bronze is an alloy of copper and:
explanation: Bronze is copper plus tin; it is used for statues and medals.

subject: Everyday Science
q: German silver contains copper, zinc and:
explanation: German silver has no silver at all; it is copper, zinc and nickel.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Solder is an alloy of lead and:
explanation: Solder (lead + tin) melts easily and joins electrical wires.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Duralumin, used in aircraft, is an alloy of aluminium with:
explanation: Duralumin is light yet strong, so it is used in aircraft bodies.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An amalgam is an alloy that contains:
explanation: Any alloy of mercury with another metal is called an amalgam.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which alloy is used for heating elements in electric heaters?
explanation: Nichrome (nickel + chromium) has high resistance and a high melting point.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bell metal is an alloy of copper and tin with:
options: A higher proportion of copper than bronze
A higher proportion of tin than bronze
explanation: Bell metal has more tin than bronze, which makes it hard and sonorous.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Gun metal is an alloy of copper, tin and:
explanation: Gun metal is copper, tin and a little zinc; it was used for guns and valves.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Oxidation is defined as:
explanation: Oxidation is loss of electrons (or gain of oxygen).

subject: Everyday Science
q: Reduction is defined as:
explanation: Reduction is gain of electrons (or loss of oxygen).

subject: Everyday Science
q: In the electrolysis of water, hydrogen gas is collected at the:
explanation: Hydrogen ions gain electrons at the cathode, forming hydrogen gas.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The volume ratio of hydrogen to oxygen obtained by electrolysis of water is:
explanation: Water is H2O, so electrolysis gives twice as much hydrogen as oxygen.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A catalyst is a substance that:
options: Speeds up a reaction without being consumed
explanation: A catalyst increases the rate of a reaction and remains unchanged.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Enzymes are:
explanation: Enzymes are protein catalysts that speed up reactions in living things.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Dry ice is solid:
explanation: Dry ice is frozen carbon dioxide, which sublimes without melting.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Laughing gas is:
explanation: Nitrous oxide, N2O, is used as an anaesthetic and is called laughing gas.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The main constituent of natural gas is:
explanation: Natural gas is mostly methane, CH4.

subject: Everyday Science
q: LPG (liquefied petroleum gas) mainly contains:
explanation: LPG is a mixture of propane and butane stored under pressure.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Marsh gas is the common name of:
explanation: Methane, produced in marshes by decaying matter, is called marsh gas.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Water gas is a mixture of:
explanation: Water gas (CO + H2) is made by passing steam over red-hot coke.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The gas used to ripen raw fruit artificially is:
explanation: Ethylene gas is used to ripen bananas and other fruit.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Carbon monoxide is poisonous because it:
options: Binds with haemoglobin and blocks oxygen
explanation: Carbon monoxide binds haemoglobin far more strongly than oxygen does.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which gas is responsible for acid rain?
explanation: Sulphur dioxide and nitrogen oxides dissolve in rain to form acids.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ozone gas has the chemical formula:
explanation: Ozone is a molecule of three oxygen atoms, O3.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The ozone layer protects life by absorbing:
explanation: The ozone layer absorbs harmful ultraviolet radiation from the Sun.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Soil erosion is mainly caused by:
explanation: Running water and wind strip away fertile topsoil.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which practice best prevents soil erosion on slopes?
explanation: Terracing and contour ploughing slow water flow and hold the soil.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Gypsum is used to reclaim:
explanation: Gypsum replaces sodium in saline soil and improves its structure.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Who is known as the father of modern chemistry?
explanation: Lavoisier named oxygen and hydrogen and stated the law of conservation of mass.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Oxygen was discovered by:
explanation: Priestley isolated oxygen in 1774; Scheele found it independently.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Hydrogen was discovered by:
explanation: Cavendish identified hydrogen as a distinct gas in 1766.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which gas is filled in electric bulbs to protect the filament?
explanation: Argon, an inert gas, fills bulbs so the hot tungsten filament does not burn in oxygen.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The electron was discovered by:
explanation: Thomson discovered the electron in 1897 using cathode rays.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Avogadro's number is approximately:
explanation: One mole of any substance contains 6.022 x 10^23 particles.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Urea, the first organic compound made in a laboratory, was synthesized by:
explanation: Wohler made urea from ammonium cyanate in 1828, founding organic synthesis.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Sulphuric acid is manufactured by the:
explanation: The contact process uses a vanadium pentoxide catalyst to make sulphuric acid.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ammonia is manufactured by the:
explanation: The Haber process combines nitrogen and hydrogen over an iron catalyst.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The main component of haemoglobin is:
explanation: Iron in haemoglobin carries oxygen in the blood.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Chlorophyll, the green pigment in plants, contains:
explanation: A magnesium atom sits at the centre of the chlorophyll molecule.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which vitamin is ascorbic acid?
explanation: Vitamin C is ascorbic acid, found in citrus fruit.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The chemical name of 'soda ash' is:
explanation: Soda ash is sodium carbonate, Na2CO3.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which acid is found in apples?
explanation: Malic acid gives apples their tart taste.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of these is a mineral acid?
explanation: Hydrochloric, sulphuric and nitric acids are mineral acids; acetic, citric and lactic are organic acids.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which organelle is known as the powerhouse of the cell?
explanation: Mitochondria release energy from food by respiration, so they are the powerhouse of the cell.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which part of the cell is called its control centre?
explanation: The nucleus holds the chromosomes and controls all cell activities.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which organelle builds proteins inside the cell?
explanation: Ribosomes build proteins by joining amino acids together.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The cell was discovered by:
explanation: Robert Hooke first saw cells in cork in 1665 and named them cells.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many chromosomes are there in a normal human body cell?
explanation: A normal human body cell has 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many chromosomes are there in a human sex cell (gamete)?
explanation: A gamete carries half the number, 23 chromosomes, so the zygote gets 46.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest cell in the human body is the:
explanation: The ovum is the largest human cell; it is just visible to the naked eye.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The smallest cell in the human body is the:
explanation: The sperm cell is the smallest human cell.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The longest cell in the human body is the:
explanation: A nerve cell can be over a metre long, running from the spinal cord to the foot.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The tissue that connects a muscle to a bone is called a:
explanation: Tendons are tough cords that join muscles to bones.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The tissue that connects one bone to another bone is called a:
explanation: Ligaments are strong bands that hold bones together at a joint.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The study of tissues is called:
explanation: Histology is the study of the microscopic structure of tissues.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The study of cells is called:
explanation: Cytology is the branch of biology that deals with cells.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The normal pH of human blood is:
explanation: Human blood is slightly alkaline, with a normal pH of about 7.4.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Blood is about what percentage of body weight?
explanation: Blood makes up about 7 to 8 percent of total body weight.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Plasma forms about what percentage of blood volume?
explanation: Blood is about 55 percent plasma and 45 percent blood cells.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The number of red blood cells in one cubic millimetre of blood is about:
explanation: There are about 5 million red blood cells in each cubic millimetre of blood.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The number of white blood cells in one cubic millimetre of blood is about:
explanation: White blood cells are far fewer than red cells, about 4,000 to 11,000 per cubic millimetre.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Platelets in the blood help in:
explanation: Platelets gather at a wound and start the clotting process.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The spleen is called the graveyard of:
explanation: Old red blood cells are broken down in the spleen, so it is called their graveyard.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The universal blood donor group is:
explanation: O negative blood has no A, B or Rh antigens, so it can be given to anyone.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The universal blood recipient group is:
explanation: AB positive blood has no antibodies against A, B or Rh, so it can receive any group.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Rh factor in blood was named after the:
explanation: The Rh factor was first found in the blood of the Rhesus monkey.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The normal heartbeat of an adult at rest is about:
explanation: A normal resting heart rate is about 72 beats per minute.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many chambers does the human heart have?
explanation: The heart has four chambers: two atria above and two ventricles below.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest artery in the human body is the:
explanation: The aorta carries blood from the left ventricle to the whole body.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest vein in the human body is the:
explanation: The inferior vena cava brings blood from the lower body back to the heart.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The valve between the left atrium and the left ventricle is the:
explanation: The mitral, or bicuspid, valve guards the opening between the left atrium and left ventricle.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The valve between the right atrium and the right ventricle is the:
explanation: The tricuspid valve has three flaps and guards the right side of the heart.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The natural pacemaker of the heart is the:
explanation: The sinoatrial (SA) node starts each heartbeat by sending an electrical impulse.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An ECG (electrocardiogram) records the:
explanation: An ECG traces the electrical signals that make the heart beat.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Normal blood pressure in a healthy adult is:
explanation: 120/80 mmHg is the standard normal blood pressure; 120 is systolic and 80 is diastolic.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The pulmonary artery carries:
explanation: The pulmonary artery is the only artery that carries deoxygenated blood, from the heart to the lungs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many bones are there in the adult human skeleton?
explanation: An adult has 206 bones; a baby is born with about 300, many of which fuse later.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The longest bone in the human body is the:
explanation: The femur, or thigh bone, is the longest and strongest bone in the body.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The smallest bone in the human body is the:
explanation: The stapes, a tiny bone in the middle ear, is the smallest bone in the body.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many bones are there in the human skull?
explanation: The skull has 22 bones: 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many vertebrae are there in the human spine?
explanation: The human backbone is made of 33 vertebrae, grouped as cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral and coccygeal.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many pairs of ribs are there in the human body?
explanation: There are 12 pairs of ribs; the first 7 pairs are true ribs attached to the sternum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many cervical vertebrae are there in the human neck?
explanation: There are 7 cervical vertebrae in the neck of humans and most mammals.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The knee joint is an example of a:
explanation: The knee bends in one direction only, like a door hinge.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The shoulder joint is an example of a:
explanation: The ball and socket joint of the shoulder allows movement in all directions.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bone cells are called:
explanation: Osteocytes are mature bone cells that maintain bone tissue.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bone marrow produces:
explanation: Red bone marrow makes red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Calcium and phosphorus are needed for healthy:
explanation: Calcium and phosphorus are the main minerals that build bones and teeth.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The strongest muscle in the human body by force is the:
explanation: The masseter, the jaw muscle, can exert the greatest force of any muscle.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest muscle in the human body is the:
explanation: The gluteus maximus, the main buttock muscle, is the largest muscle in the body.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Voluntary muscles are also called:
explanation: Skeletal muscles are attached to bones and move when we choose to move them.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The number of muscles in the human body is about:
explanation: There are about 600 muscles in the human body, making up nearly half its weight.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Muscle fatigue is caused by the accumulation of:
explanation: During hard exercise, muscles produce lactic acid, which causes tiredness and cramps.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Cardiac muscle is found in the:
explanation: Cardiac muscle is the special involuntary muscle that makes the heart beat.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The human brain weighs about:
explanation: An adult human brain weighs about 1.3 to 1.4 kg, around 2 percent of body weight.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest part of the human brain is the:
explanation: The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain; it controls thought, memory and voluntary action.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Balance and coordination of the body are controlled by the:
explanation: The cerebellum, at the back of the brain, keeps balance and coordinates movement.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The medulla oblongata controls:
explanation: The medulla controls involuntary actions such as heartbeat, breathing and swallowing.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many pairs of cranial nerves are there in humans?
explanation: There are 12 pairs of cranial nerves, which arise directly from the brain.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many pairs of spinal nerves are there in humans?
explanation: There are 31 pairs of spinal nerves arising from the spinal cord.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The basic unit of the nervous system is the:
explanation: Neurons are nerve cells that carry messages as electrical impulses.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The gap between two neurons is called a:
explanation: A synapse is the small gap across which a nerve signal passes from one neuron to the next.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The human brain uses about what percentage of the body's oxygen?
explanation: Although the brain is only about 2 percent of body weight, it uses about 20 percent of the oxygen we take in.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A reflex action, such as pulling the hand away from a hot object, is controlled by the:
explanation: Reflex actions are quick automatic responses controlled by the spinal cord, without waiting for the brain.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Body temperature is controlled by the:
explanation: The hypothalamus acts as the body's thermostat and also controls hunger and thirst.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Cerebrospinal fluid protects the:
explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid cushions the brain and spinal cord against shocks.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The human brain has how many hemispheres?
explanation: The cerebrum is divided into two hemispheres, left and right, joined by the corpus callosum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Rods in the retina of the eye help us to see in:
explanation: Rods are sensitive to low light; cones work in bright light and detect colour.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Cones in the retina of the eye help in:
explanation: Cones in the retina detect colour and fine detail in bright light.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The blind spot of the eye is the point where the:
explanation: There are no rods or cones where the optic nerve leaves the eye, so that spot cannot see.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The iris of the eye controls the:
explanation: The iris opens and closes to change the size of the pupil and control how much light enters.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In the human eye, the image is formed on the:
explanation: The lens focuses light onto the retina, where rods and cones turn it into nerve signals.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In myopia (short sight), a person can see clearly:
options: Near objects, but not distant objects
Distant objects, but not near objects
explanation: In myopia the eyeball is too long, so distant images fall in front of the retina and look blurred.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The most common type of colour blindness is:
explanation: Most colour-blind people cannot tell red from green; it is more common in men.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The eardrum is also called the:
explanation: The tympanic membrane vibrates when sound waves strike it.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The cochlea in the inner ear is concerned with:
explanation: The cochlea turns sound vibrations into nerve signals that the brain hears.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The semicircular canals in the ear help in:
explanation: The three semicircular canals sense the movement of the head and help keep balance.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The number of taste buds on the human tongue is about:
explanation: There are about 10,000 taste buds on the tongue, most of which are replaced every two weeks.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Sweet taste is detected mainly at the:
explanation: Sweet taste buds are concentrated at the tip of the tongue.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest organ of the human body is the:
explanation: The skin is the largest organ, covering about 2 square metres in an adult.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Digestion of food begins in the:
explanation: Digestion starts in the mouth, where teeth chew food and saliva begins to break down starch.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Saliva contains the enzyme:
explanation: Salivary amylase (ptyalin) begins the digestion of starch in the mouth.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest gland in the human body is the:
explanation: The liver is the largest gland and the largest internal organ, weighing about 1.5 kg.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bile is produced by the:
explanation: The liver makes bile, which helps digest fats; the gall bladder only stores it.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bile is stored in the:
explanation: Bile made by the liver is stored and concentrated in the gall bladder.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Insulin is produced by the:
explanation: The beta cells of the pancreas produce insulin, which lowers blood sugar.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Diabetes is caused by the lack of:
explanation: When the pancreas makes too little insulin, blood sugar rises and diabetes results.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The length of the small intestine in an adult is about:
explanation: The small intestine is about 6 to 7 metres long and is where most digestion and absorption happen.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Villi absorb digested food in the:
explanation: Tiny finger-like villi line the small intestine and absorb nutrients into the blood.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An adult human has how many teeth?
explanation: An adult has 32 permanent teeth, including 4 wisdom teeth.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The normal breathing rate of an adult at rest is:
explanation: A healthy adult breathes about 12 to 16 times a minute at rest.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Exchange of gases in the lungs takes place in the:
explanation: The alveoli are tiny air sacs where oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide leaves it.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The windpipe is also called the:
explanation: The trachea, or windpipe, carries air from the throat down to the lungs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The voice box is called the:
explanation: The larynx holds the vocal cords, which vibrate to produce the voice.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The right lung has how many lobes?
explanation: The right lung has 3 lobes and the left lung has 2, leaving room for the heart.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Urea is formed in the:
explanation: The liver converts excess amino acids into urea, which the kidneys then remove.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Urine is stored in the:
explanation: Urine made by the kidneys travels down the ureters and is stored in the bladder.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The kidneys filter the:
explanation: The kidneys filter waste such as urea from the blood and make urine.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Herpetology is the study of:
explanation: Herpetology deals with reptiles and amphibians; birds are studied in ornithology.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Night blindness is caused by the deficiency of:
explanation: Vitamin A is needed for vision in dim light; its deficiency causes night blindness.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Beriberi is caused by the deficiency of:
explanation: Lack of vitamin B1 (thiamine) causes beriberi, which weakens the muscles and nerves.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Goitre is caused by the deficiency of:
explanation: Lack of iodine swells the thyroid gland, causing goitre; iodized salt prevents it.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Anaemia is caused by the deficiency of:
explanation: Iron is needed to make haemoglobin; too little iron causes anaemia, with pale skin and tiredness.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A doctor uses a stethoscope to listen to the sounds of the:
explanation: A stethoscope lets a doctor hear the heartbeat and the sounds of breathing in the lungs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A glucometer is used to measure the level of:
explanation: A glucometer measures glucose (sugar) in the blood; diabetics use it to check their sugar level.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A spirometer is used to measure the:
explanation: A spirometer measures how much air the lungs can hold and how fast air can be breathed out.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An endoscope is an instrument used to:
explanation: An endoscope is a thin tube with a camera that lets a doctor see inside the stomach, intestines or other hollow organs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An otoscope is used by a doctor to examine the:
explanation: An otoscope is a small lighted instrument for looking into the ear canal and at the eardrum.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An ophthalmoscope is used to examine the inside of the:
explanation: An ophthalmoscope lets a doctor look at the retina and blood vessels at the back of the eye.

subject: Everyday Science
q: An electron microscope uses a beam of:
explanation: An electron microscope uses a beam of electrons instead of light, so it can magnify things up to a million times.

subject: Everyday Science
q: SONAR stands for:
explanation: SONAR uses sound waves to find objects under water; ships and submarines use it to detect objects and measure depth.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In medicine, ultrasound (sonography) is used to:
options: Make images of organs inside the body
explanation: Sonography uses harmless ultrasound waves to make pictures of a baby in the womb and of organs such as the liver and kidneys.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A rain gauge is used to measure the amount of:
explanation: A rain gauge is a simple open container that collects rain so the depth of rainfall can be measured.

subject: Everyday Science
q: MRI stands for:
explanation: MRI uses strong magnets and radio waves to make detailed pictures of soft tissues such as the brain and muscles.

subject: Everyday Science
q: CT scan stands for:
explanation: A CT scan uses many X-ray pictures taken from different angles and a computer to build a 3-D image of the body.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bats are the only mammals that can:
explanation: Bats are the only mammals capable of true flight; their wings are made of skin stretched over long finger bones.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Bats are mostly active at:
explanation: Bats are nocturnal animals; they sleep in dark places during the day and fly out at night to feed.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A group of bats living together is called a:
explanation: Bats roost together in large groups called colonies, often in caves, trees or old buildings.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Dolphins find their food and navigate under water by using:
explanation: Like bats, dolphins send out sounds and listen to the echoes to locate fish and objects in murky water.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of these animals can hear ultrasound?
explanation: Dogs can hear sounds above 20,000 Hz that humans cannot hear, which is why dog whistles work silently for us.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Elephants communicate over long distances using:
explanation: Elephants produce very low sounds below 20 Hz (infrasound) that travel for kilometres through the ground and air.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ultrasound is used in industry to:
explanation: High-frequency sound waves shake off dirt from delicate objects such as jewellery, lenses and surgical tools without damaging them.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Fruit bats help plants by:
explanation: Fruit bats carry pollen from flower to flower and drop seeds far from the parent tree, helping forests to grow.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest bird in the world is the:
explanation: The ostrich is the largest living bird; it can be about 2.7 metres tall and weigh over 150 kg.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The ostrich is a flightless bird, but it is the:
explanation: An ostrich cannot fly, but it can run at up to 70 km per hour, faster than any other bird on land.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest egg laid by any living bird is the egg of the:
explanation: An ostrich egg is about 15 cm long and weighs about 1.4 kg, the largest egg of any living bird.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many toes does an ostrich have on each foot?
explanation: The ostrich is the only bird with just two toes on each foot, which helps it run fast across the ground.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The penguin is a bird that cannot fly but is an excellent:
explanation: Penguins use their wings as flippers to swim fast under water, catching fish and krill.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest species of penguin is the:
explanation: The emperor penguin, found in Antarctica, is the tallest and heaviest of all penguins, standing about 1.2 metres tall.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The kiwi, a flightless bird, is the national bird of:
explanation: The kiwi is a small flightless bird of New Zealand and is the country's national symbol.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The hummingbird is the smallest bird and the only bird that can:
explanation: A hummingbird can hover in the air and even fly backwards, beating its wings about 80 times a second.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The fastest bird in the world when diving is the:
explanation: The peregrine falcon dives at more than 300 km per hour, making it the fastest animal in the world.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The bird with the largest wingspan in the world is the:
explanation: The wandering albatross has a wingspan of up to 3.5 metres, the largest of any living bird.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Photosynthesis takes place mainly in the:
explanation: Photosynthesis happens in the green leaves, inside tiny structures called chloroplasts that contain chlorophyll.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In photosynthesis, plants produce:
explanation: Plants use sunlight, water and carbon dioxide to make glucose food and release oxygen into the air.

subject: Everyday Science
q: During photosynthesis, plants take in carbon dioxide and give out:
explanation: Plants absorb carbon dioxide from the air and release oxygen, which is why forests are called the lungs of the Earth.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Chlorophyll, the green pigment of plants, mainly absorbs:
explanation: Chlorophyll absorbs red and blue light for photosynthesis and reflects green light, which is why leaves look green.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Stomata are tiny pores on the leaves used for:
explanation: Stomata open and close to let carbon dioxide in and oxygen and water vapour out of the leaf.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The xylem in a plant carries:
options: Water from the roots to the leaves
Food from the leaves to the roots
explanation: Xylem vessels carry water and dissolved minerals upward from the roots to the leaves.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The phloem in a plant carries:
options: Water from the roots to the leaves
Food from the leaves to other parts
explanation: Phloem tubes carry the food made in the leaves to the growing parts and storage organs of the plant.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Transpiration is the loss of water from a plant in the form of:
explanation: Transpiration is the evaporation of water vapour through the stomata of the leaves; it also pulls water up from the roots.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from the anther to the:
explanation: Pollination moves pollen from the male anther to the female stigma of a flower, carried by insects, wind or water.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A seed needs which of these to germinate?
explanation: A seed germinates when it gets water, oxygen from the air and a suitable warm temperature.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest flower in the world is the:
explanation: Rafflesia, found in the rainforests of Southeast Asia, can grow over one metre across and smells like rotting meat.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The fastest-growing plant in the world is:
explanation: Bamboo, a type of grass, can grow nearly one metre in a single day under the right conditions.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The potato is an underground:
explanation: A potato is a swollen underground stem called a tuber; its eyes are buds that can grow into new plants.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of these is a root eaten as a vegetable?
explanation: A carrot is a swollen tap root; a potato is a stem and an onion is a bulb, while ginger is a rhizome stem.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The spines of a cactus are modified:
explanation: Cactus spines are leaves changed into sharp points to reduce water loss and protect the plant from animals.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The Venus flytrap is a plant that:
explanation: The Venus flytrap is an insect-eating plant; its leaves snap shut when an insect touches the tiny hairs inside.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Gymnosperms, such as pine and deodar, are plants whose seeds are:
explanation: Gymnosperms bear naked seeds on cones; their seeds are not enclosed inside a fruit like those of flowering plants.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The age of a tree can be found by counting its:
explanation: Each year a tree adds one ring of wood; counting the rings in the trunk tells how old the tree is.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ecology is the study of:
explanation: Ecology studies how living things interact with each other and with their surroundings.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A food chain always begins with:
explanation: Every food chain starts with green plants, which make their own food by photosynthesis and feed all other life.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In the food chain grass - grasshopper - frog - snake - hawk, the frog is a:
explanation: The grasshopper eats the grass (primary consumer) and the frog eats the grasshopper, so the frog is a secondary consumer.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Decomposers in an ecosystem are mainly:
explanation: Bacteria and fungi break down dead plants and animals, returning nutrients to the soil for new plants to use.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The biosphere is the part of the Earth where:
explanation: The biosphere is the zone of land, water and air where living things are found, from deep oceans to high mountains.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A biome is a large region with similar:
explanation: A biome, such as a desert, forest or tundra, is a large area with a similar climate and the plants and animals suited to it.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The natural home of an organism is called its:
explanation: A habitat is the place where an organism lives and finds food, water and shelter, such as a pond or a forest.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A population in ecology means a group of organisms of:
options: The same species living in one area
Plants and animals of a desert
explanation: A population is all the members of one species, such as all the frogs in a pond, living in the same place.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Leguminous plants, such as peas and beans, help the soil by:
explanation: Leguminous plants work with Rhizobium bacteria in their root nodules to fix nitrogen gas from the air into the soil.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The water cycle consists of evaporation, condensation and:
explanation: Water evaporates from seas and land, condenses into clouds, and falls back as rain or snow (precipitation).

subject: Everyday Science
q: Which of these gases causes the greenhouse effect?
explanation: Carbon dioxide and methane trap heat in the atmosphere, warming the Earth like the glass of a greenhouse.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest ecosystem on Earth is the:
explanation: The ocean covers about 71 percent of the Earth's surface and is the largest ecosystem, home to most of the world's life.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest animal in the world is the:
explanation: The blue whale can grow to about 30 metres long and weigh 180 tonnes, larger than any dinosaur ever found.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The blue whale is a:
explanation: The blue whale is a mammal; it breathes air through a blowhole and feeds its baby with milk.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The fastest land animal in the world is the:
explanation: The cheetah can run at about 100 km per hour in short bursts, faster than any other land animal.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The tallest land animal in the world is the:
explanation: A giraffe can stand about 5.5 metres tall; its long neck has only seven vertebrae, just like a human neck.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The largest land animal in the world is the:
explanation: The African elephant is the largest land animal, weighing up to 6 tonnes and standing about 3.5 metres tall.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The kangaroo is a marsupial, which means its baby:
explanation: Marsupials such as kangaroos carry their tiny babies in a pouch, where the joey feeds and grows.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The platypus is unusual because it is a mammal that:
explanation: The platypus is a mammal that lays eggs and has a duck-like bill; it lives in the rivers of Australia.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A dolphin breathes air through a hole on top of its head called a:
explanation: Dolphins are mammals and must come to the surface to breathe through the blowhole on top of their heads.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The skeleton of a shark is made of:
explanation: Sharks have no true bones; their skeletons are made of cartilage, the same flexible tissue found in the human nose.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A snake uses its forked tongue mainly to:
explanation: A snake flicks its forked tongue to pick up scent particles from the air and carry them to a special sense organ.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A frog is an amphibian because it can live:
options: Both in water and on land
explanation: Frogs begin life as tadpoles in water and grow into adults that live on land, breathing through lungs and moist skin.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Fish breathe under water through their:
explanation: Fish take oxygen from the water through feathery gills on the sides of their heads.

subject: Everyday Science
q: How many hearts does an octopus have?
explanation: An octopus has three hearts: two pump blood to the gills and one pumps blood to the rest of the body.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A starfish can regrow a lost arm because of its power of:
explanation: Starfish can regenerate, or grow back, arms that are broken off, and in some species a lost arm can grow a whole new starfish.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Gregor Mendel is known as the father of:
explanation: Gregor Mendel discovered the laws of heredity through his experiments on pea plants in the 1860s.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Mendel carried out his famous experiments on:
explanation: Mendel crossed pea plants with different traits, such as tall and short, and worked out how traits are passed on.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A gene is the basic unit of:
explanation: A gene is a section of DNA that carries the instructions for one inherited trait, such as eye colour.

subject: Everyday Science
q: DNA stands for:
explanation: DNA (deoxyribonucleic acid) carries all the genetic instructions for building and running a living thing.

subject: Everyday Science
q: DNA is found mainly in the:
explanation: Most of a cell's DNA is stored in the nucleus, coiled into structures called chromosomes.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Genes are carried on structures in the nucleus called:
explanation: Chromosomes are thread-like structures made of DNA and protein; they carry the genes from parents to children.

subject: Everyday Science
q: In mitosis, one cell divides into:
explanation: Mitosis is the cell division used for growth and repair; it produces two daughter cells identical to the parent cell.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Meiosis is the cell division that produces:
options: Four cells with half the chromosomes
explanation: Meiosis produces four gametes (sex cells), each with half the number of chromosomes, so a child gets a full set from both parents.

subject: Everyday Science
q: A mutation is a sudden change in the:
explanation: A mutation is a change in the DNA of an organism; it can be caused by radiation or chemicals and may be passed to offspring.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Identical twins develop from:
explanation: Identical twins come from one fertilised egg that splits into two, so they share the same genes and look alike.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Tuberculosis (TB) is caused by a:
explanation: Tuberculosis is caused by the bacterium Mycobacterium tuberculosis, which mainly attacks the lungs.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Cholera is a disease caused by a bacterium and spreads mainly through:
explanation: Cholera is caused by the bacterium Vibrio cholerae and spreads when people drink water polluted with sewage.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Typhoid fever is caused by the bacterium:
explanation: Typhoid is caused by Salmonella typhi and spreads through contaminated food and water.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Malaria is caused by the parasite Plasmodium and is spread by the:
explanation: The female Anopheles mosquito carries the Plasmodium parasite in its saliva and passes it to people when it bites.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Dengue fever is spread by the bite of the:
explanation: Dengue is a viral disease spread by the Aedes mosquito, which bites during the daytime.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Hepatitis is a viral disease that mainly affects the:
explanation: Hepatitis viruses infect the liver, causing jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes) and weakness.

subject: Everyday Science
q: AIDS is caused by HIV, a virus that attacks the body's:
explanation: HIV destroys the white blood cells that defend the body, so the immune system can no longer fight infections.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Ringworm is a skin infection caused by a:
explanation: Ringworm is caused by fungi that grow on the skin, forming round red itchy patches; it is not caused by a worm.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Amoebic dysentery is caused by:
explanation: Amoebic dysentery is caused by the microscopic organism Entamoeba histolytica, spread through contaminated food and water.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Antibiotics are medicines that kill:
explanation: Antibiotics kill bacteria, but they do not work against viruses, so a cold or flu cannot be cured with antibiotics.

subject: Everyday Science
q: The pituitary gland is called the master gland because it:
explanation: The pituitary gland, at the base of the brain, releases hormones that control the thyroid, adrenals and other glands.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Adrenaline is known as the emergency hormone because it:
options: Prepares the body for fight or flight
explanation: Adrenaline is released in danger or stress; it speeds up the heartbeat and sends more blood to the muscles.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Thyroxine, produced by the thyroid gland, controls the body's:
explanation: Thyroxine controls how fast the body uses energy; too little of it slows the body and too much speeds it up.

subject: Everyday Science
q: Growth hormone, which controls the growth of the body, is produced by the:
explanation: Growth hormone from the pituitary gland controls the growth of bones and muscles, especially in children.
